catalog_quote: [Bridgeman 1961:333, page image opened] 3. The third emic system of the Kaiwá phonological structure is that of the paralinguistic features of stress and rhythm. 3.1. Two degrees of stress inter-act in Kaiwá discourse. 3.1.1. Lexical stress usually occurs on the stem final syllable of isolation forms: ejuvi you strangle something, eju-vi you come here for a short time; ajepota I light a fire, ajepo-ta I will jump. In loan words and some apparently native words stress is on the penult: háša hatchet, ója kettle, áva man. In context lexical stress is sometimes perturbed. When stress occurs other than word final it is marked by ′. 3.1.2. Sentence stress, marked ″, is illustrated by the following pairs of examples. ... new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed for this languoid, so there were not two silent/unopened works to spot-check. In their place I searched the rest of the same volume for Kaiwá (one hit, p. 129, sound correspondences only) and a full-text search for stress/accent the non-listed Carvalho 2018 UnB thesis already in the folder (3 hits: 'acento [-nasal]' twice on the same passage, meaning the nasal feature of a stem, not stress; and the bibliography entry 'BRIDGEMAN, L. I. A note on stress in Kaiwá. 1960. Arquivo Linguistico no 225'). Nothing about stress placement was missed; Bridgeman 1960 remains the unobtained placement source.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on the page scan we hold of Bridgeman 1961 p. 333 (sec. 3.1.1-3.1.2), locator correct; strength of the evidence 'page-image' is accurate. Deciding source: a 1961 IJAL phonology article by the primary fieldworker, the only phonology-typed reference Glottolog lists for Kaiwá; the held grammar (Cardoso 2008) and sketch (Taylor & Taylor 1966) are silent on stress, and the one open item I could download now (de Carvalho 2018 UnB thesis) is also silent. The 'morphological' (stem-final, suffixes like -vi, -ta outside the stress domain; lexical penult exceptions háša, ója, áva) reading follows directly from Bridgeman's wording 'stem final syllable of isolation forms'
